name: Pedro Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a continuous miner at the Northfield potash mine, about a kilometre underground. It's a long machine with a spinning drum full of teeth at the front, and it cuts the potash ore straight off the face and loads it onto conveyors behind. I lead a cutting crew of four and I'm the one who trains the apprentices on the miner. I love a good long cut where the drum sings and the floor stays level, and I hate the heat at the face in summer, and the paperwork.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been training apprentices?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About eight years now. I came up through an apprenticeship myself, and an old operator called Viktor taught me everything, so I see it as paying it back. My wife Leila runs a small daycare from our house, and we've got Omar, who's sixteen, and Sara, who's eleven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise. I'd say that at work and to the brothers at the mosque on Friday, with a bit of a smile. Real work is still done by real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things go on as they are. I keep my crew, keep training the young ones, and pay off the house slowly. I'd be content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I use the AI app now and then to write up the apprentices' assessments, so I'd keep doing that. We'd keep saving our usual amount, and Omar's apprenticeship plans wouldn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are Omar's plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants to be an electrician, and I've told him the mine takes apprentices every January. I'd be proud to see him underground with a hard hat on, but in a safer job than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd change, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The remote monitoring they put on the miner two years ago. It's good, it tells me if a bearing's getting hot. I'd like more of that, not less, but I want it as a helper, not a boss.

S0.say: I'd say at work and to the brothers at the mosque, with a smile, that it was a lot of noise. Real work is still done by real people.
S0.think: Things go on as they are: I keep my crew, keep training the young ones and slowly pay off the house. I'd be content.
S0.do: Keeps working and training apprentices, and keeps using the AI app now and then for their assessments. Keeps saving the usual amount and supports his son's plan for an electrical apprenticeship at the mine.
S0.quote: I want it as a helper, not a boss.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro sees technology as useful when it serves the operator. His identity is tied to training apprentices, as he was trained himself. His son's apprenticeship plan is a family anchor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of mining and always has been. The companies have the right to bring in better machines, but they should bring their people with them. I'd say a good apprenticeship is worth more than any government scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the miner becomes remote-controlled from the surface within a few years. That means one person runs two or three machines, so fewer crew leads. I'd be okay, I think, because I know the machine, but some of my crew wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be trained on the remote system as soon as it's proven at another mine. I'd keep teaching apprentices, but I'd teach them the remote side too. We'd put an extra bit away, maybe 150 a fortnight, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I trust that good workers find a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jamal, my youngest apprentice, he's 19 and just started. He's sharp but he's at the bottom of the list. I'd make sure he gets the remote training too, so he's not first out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push Omar away from the mine in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd tell him to make sure his electrical ticket covers automation. Every new machine still needs someone to wire it.

S1.say: I'd say change has always been part of mining and companies have the right to bring in better machines, but they should bring their people too. A good apprenticeship beats any government scheme.
S1.think: Privately I think the miner goes remote within a few years, with one person running two or three machines. I'd be okay because I know the machine, but some of my crew wouldn't.
S1.do: Asks for training on the remote system once it's proven at another mine and teaches apprentices the remote side too. Puts an extra 150 a fortnight into savings just in case.
S1.feel: Uneasy but steady, trusting that good workers find a place.
S1.quote: Every new machine still needs someone to wire it.
S1.fieldNote: Pedro accepts the company's right to automate but expects loyalty in return. His concern is his youngest apprentice, who would be first out. He'd adapt once he sees it work elsewhere, which fits his steady nature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and it will break families. I wouldn't say the government should pay everyone, but it should slow things down so people can adjust. I'd say that at work and at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone, and Omar's apprenticeship might be gone before he finishes it. That hurts more than my own job. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away, the new car and the trip to see Leila's family would wait. I'd tell Omar to pick a trade where people want a person, maybe gas fitting in homes. Leila's daycare might grow, so I'd help her with the business side and the building work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake thinking about Omar more than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years let you do that you couldn't do with none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get some money in the bank and get Omar pointed in a better direction. That's about it. You can't build a new life in two years with a mortgage and kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government support if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my family needed it, yes, but only as a bridge. I'd want it tied to work or training. I'd feel ashamed to just sit.

S2.say: I'd say at work and at the mosque that it's too fast and will break families. The government shouldn't pay everyone, but it should slow things down so people can adjust.
S2.think: Off the record I think my job is gone, and Omar's apprenticeship might vanish before he finishes. That hurts more than my own job.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once, delaying the new car and the trip to his wife's family. Steers his son toward a trade like home gas fitting and helps grow his wife's daycare business.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, more over his son than himself.
S2.quote: Omar's apprenticeship might be gone before he finishes it. That hurts more than my own job.
S2.fieldNote: Pedro's sharpest pain in the fast scenario is for his son's future, not his own job. He'd accept government help only as a bridge tied to work. His wife's daycare becomes the family's possible lifeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years and we should use them to train people, not to argue. I'd tell the company to start apprenticeships in the new work right now. I'd say families should get their houses in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me 48. I think I'd keep the miner for two or three years and then go into training people on the new systems, if the company lets me. After that, I'm not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the remote operations course in year one, once a couple of others at the mine had done it. I'd ask the training department about moving across. We'd pay the mortgage harder and keep about five months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's real, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can follow the path I know. With two I'm grabbing at anything, with five I can move into training like I always half wanted. And Omar can finish his ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'after that, I'm not sure'. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I don't like not knowing. But I've never known what's in ten years, really, and God has looked after us so far.

S3.say: I'd say we should use the few years to train people, not to argue. The company should start apprenticeships in the new work now, and families should get their houses in order.
S3.think: At 48 I'd keep the miner for two or three years, then move into training people on the new systems if allowed. After that I'm not sure.
S3.do: Takes the remote operations course in year one once colleagues have tested it, and asks to move into the training department. Pays the mortgage harder and holds about five months of savings.
S3.feel: Anxious, but able to see a path.
S3.quote: With two I'm grabbing at anything, with five I can move into training like I always half wanted.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Pedro follow a path he already half wanted, moving into training. He is uneasy about what comes after and leans on faith. He still waits for colleagues to go first on new courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it properly with apprenticeships. I'd say the companies and the trade schools should work together. People should stand on their own feet with the right skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years makes me 53. I think I'd be fine, moving into training and maybe running courses for other mines. Omar would be established by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the miner for a few years and start teaching evening courses at the trade college. Maybe build that into a small business training operators across mines. We'd aim to have the house nearly paid off by 50.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly in the background. It's a long road but I know where it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't there a risk the trade college jobs go too, in the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But people will want to learn from a person for a long time, I think. When Viktor taught me, it wasn't the facts, it was how he stood at the face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your apprentices in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn everything, the old way and the new way. Be the one who knows why the machine does what it does. And look after each other.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty to do it properly with apprenticeships, with companies and trade schools working together. People should stand on their own feet with the right skills.
S4.think: At 53 I think I'd be fine, moving into training and maybe running courses for other mines. Omar would be established by then.
S4.do: Keeps the miner for a few years while teaching evening courses at the trade college. Builds that into a small business training operators across mines and aims to nearly pay off the house by 50.
S4.feel: Uneasy only in the background, sure of where the road goes.
S4.quote: When Viktor taught me, it wasn't the facts, it was how he stood at the face.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Pedro turns his mentoring into a possible business. He believes people will still want to learn from people. His values of self-reliance and apprenticeship shape every plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of Omar. My life is mostly built, his isn't. What would help is the companies keeping apprenticeships open in whatever new jobs there are, and help for grown men to retrain without losing the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about pride. A man who's worked underground for twenty years doesn't want a cheque, he wants to be useful. Whatever the plan is, give people something to do.

headlineQuote: My life is mostly built, his isn't.
portrait: Pedro Khan is a 43-year-old continuous miner operator and crew lead at the Northfield underground potash mine, who has trained apprentices for eight years the way an old operator once trained him. He is married to Leila, who runs a home daycare, and they have a teenage son planning an electrical apprenticeship and a younger daughter. He uses AI now and then and adopts new tools once proven, believing companies may automate but owe their people training. In the two-year AGI picture he is alarmed mostly for his son, while with five or ten years he plans to move into training and perhaps run courses for other mines.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because his son's life isn't built yet and his apprenticeship could disappear.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping apprenticeships open in the new jobs, and help for adults to retrain without losing their homes.
